Triggers.value: Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to erase the memory of the event
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

I have failed in my most important role in life
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: 'Being in nature similar to where it happened' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of life-threatening illness, which typically involves medical/health contexts rather than a natural-environment trauma setting.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid grief reminders' implies bereavement/loss of another person, which does not fit the stated trauma type of life-threatening illness unless there is an unreported death-related trauma; it is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: 'Fear of rage' is weakly connected to the rest of the profile: the other appraisals and memory items center on damage, unreality, and role failure after illness, not anger-based dyscontrol. This makes the appraisal set less internally coherent.

vignette:
Mina Tran was a 42-year-old married project manager who came to treatment after months of trying to keep her life moving as if nothing had happened, even while feeling increasingly overwhelmed by a story she could scarcely hold in mind. A South Eastern Asian American woman who had built her work around planning, deadlines, and calm problem-solving, she spoke about the year of her illness as though it belonged to someone else. When she described the period before her hospitalization, she could recount certain moments with startling clarity - the chill in the emergency room, the metallic smell that seemed to cling to the air, the sight of needles and IV drips threading into her arm - yet whole stretches of time were blank for her, as if they had been wiped away. She said that what remained was so extreme that it was hard to believe it had actually happened to her. At times she did not picture a coherent scene at all; instead, a wave of terror and helplessness would arrive in her body with no clear image attached, leaving her shaken by emotion alone.

Mina's illness had begun with symptoms she initially minimized, but it escalated until she needed emergency medical care and then a hospital admission that she experienced as life-threatening. The practical details of being monitored, punctured, and surrounded by equipment became the center of her memory. She recalled the coldness of the room and the cold temperature of the sheets against her skin, and those sensations now remained potent reminders. Even months later, a blast of cold air from an office vent, a refrigerated aisle at the grocery store, or stepping outside on an unexpectedly chilly morning could make her tense and feel abruptly pulled back toward that time. The smell of disinfectant in a clinic, alcohol swabs, or the particular sterile odor that drifted from a medical office would do the same. So would the sight of needles, drips, and tubing in hospitals, ambulances, or even routine physical examinations. She said that when she saw medical equipment, her body reacted before she had a chance to think, and she would feel a familiar surge of dread and urgency to get away.

In the months after she returned home, Mina began organizing her days around keeping those reminders out of reach. She stopped going to the hospital even for issues she knew should probably be checked, and she delayed routine physical examinations because she could not tolerate the waiting rooms, the smell, or the possibility of seeing equipment on a cart. She also tried to erase the memory of the event by pushing away any thought connected to it, telling herself that if she could just refuse it enough, it would disappear. Instead, she found herself constantly scanning her own thoughts for signs that she was "going crazy," worried that the incomplete, unreal quality of the memory meant something was wrong with her mind. This monitoring became a private habit, carried out silently while she was at her desk or in conversations with her husband, as if she had to keep checking whether her thoughts were still orderly.

As a project manager, Mina depended on being present, responsive, and steady, but the practical consequences of avoiding medical cues had begun to intrude on work and daily life. She scheduled meetings carefully so she would not have to pass the clinic attached to her office building, and she chose routes that kept her away from the nearby ambulance bay. She noticed herself declining invitations that might involve a health center, and she became increasingly uneasy when colds, air conditioning, or lingering antiseptic smells were unavoidable. Her husband had begun to notice how often she seemed preoccupied and how quickly she would withdraw when anything reminded her of the hospital. Mina herself spoke with a heavy conviction that her life had been destroyed by the trauma, and that her body had been permanently damaged by what happened to her. She said this with a flat certainty that seemed to leave little room for reassurance, as if the illness had not only threatened her life at the time but had also altered what she could trust about her own physical safety now.

What brought Mina to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulation of these experiences until she could no longer keep them hidden. She was tired of policing her own mind, tired of arranging her work and errands around hospitals she did not want to see, and tired of being ambushed by smell, cold, and medical equipment in ordinary places. She did not say she wanted to forget that her illness had happened so much as to stop feeling as though it was happening again whenever a reminder appeared. What frightened her most was that the memory remained partly blank and partly vivid, and that her body could still react with such force to a smell, a chill, or the sight of a needle. What she hoped for was a way to live in the present without constantly bracing for the return of something she had survived but still experienced as devastating and unreal.
